title: Candomblé and Capoeira: Saying What It Is For

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *para que* + subjunctive from B1 Unit 4: it says the purpose of an action, with a new subject in the second clause (*Te llamo para que vengas*). When the subject stays the same, you know *para* + infinitive. Purposes are everywhere in Bahian culture: why a drum is played, why a game was disguised. Here the structure works on Candomblé and capoeira.

sections.title: Purpose with para que
rows: Se tocan los atabaques para que el orixá llegue al terreiro.
*para que* + present subjunctive: the drums are for the orixá to arrive
Los esclavizados practicaban la capoeira como baile para que los capataces no la prohibieran.
*para que* + imperfect subjunctive after a past verb
Hoy se enseña capoeira para que los jóvenes conozcan esta historia.
a new subject: the young people
Los maestros enseñan capoeira para transmitir esta tradición.

items.spanish: Los devotos llevan ofrendas para que la fiesta salga bien.
items.english: The devotees bring offerings so that the festival goes well.

items.spanish: El maestro toca el berimbau para que los jugadores empiecen.
items.english: The master plays the berimbau so that the players start.

items.spanish: Se escondía la lucha bajo el baile para que nadie sospechara.
items.english: The fight was hidden under the dance so that nobody would suspect.

sections.content: After *para que*, the verb is always subjunctive: present for a present or future purpose, imperfect after a past verb (*para que no la prohibieran*). If the same person does both actions, use *para* + infinitive, not *para que*.
